version_history.subject: [RFC PATCH 0/1] mm/swap: keep reclaim batches contiguous on swap

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 1/1] mm/swap: allocate contiguous swap slots for a reclaim batch
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes swap slot allocation by allocating contiguous slots in batches, reducing the number of small write requests and improving performance. It achieves this by recording the number of pages of each order that need a slot before swapping out a batch, and then making those allocations follow contiguous free slots. This approach helps to minimize the fragmentation of swap clusters and reduces the overhead of small write requests.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concerns that the patch does not address workloads that benefit more from disk swapping than compression swapping, and requested further consideration for these use cases.

Reviewer noted that the patch does not apply its contiguous allocation heuristic to folios larger than a certain order, and found this omission reasonable.

Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concern that the patch's preference for non-full clusters with contiguous slots may lead to increased lock contention, especially as swapfiles become more fragmented.

Reviewer Nhat Pham raised concerns about the effectiveness of the contiguous swap slot allocation heuristic, questioning whether it would lead to overshooting the estimate and creating problems down the line. They also suggested that this heuristic might not be necessary for cgroups that enable zswap or zram.
review_comments.raw_body:
Thanks for looking into this! There are still workloads that benefit
more from disk swapping than compression swapping... We should make
the swap subsystem work for them.

I haven't read the code too closely, as it's an RFC meant to show the
general idea. So I'll just make some comments and ask some questions
about the idea:

---

Ah so we don't invoke this heuristics for folio larger than certain
orders? Makes sense.

---

So we prefer non-full clusters with contiguous slots, over free
clusters, over other nonfull clusters.

I think this part makes sense to me FWIW. We do skip fast path and go
for slow paths more often, so do make sure we're not paying with too
much lock contention, especially as the swapfile fils or get more
fragmented (which this patch series does nudge us towards). But FWIW,
we pretty much go back to the old behavior the moment we fail to find
contiguity for the first time in the batch, so I think we'll be
fine...?

---

Some general questions:

1. How many pages in folio_list typically do get reclaimed? There can
be quite a few with references, which we rotate/promote, when we scan,
right? Would constantly overshooting the estimate create problem down
the line?

(This is one of the few places where indirection (vswap) would have
helped - we can collect a batch of pages after unmapping, then pass
them to the phys swap allocator (after checking zswappability, etc.).
Maybe we can solve it better after it's landed, and accept an
imperfect solution for now?)

2. Should we skip this heuristics for cgroups that enables zswap (and
maybe zram)? Contiguity matters less there... unless it help at
writeback time? Hard to say without experimentation - maybe you can do
the same check you did for your zswap writeback batching patch series?

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch aims to reduce the number of I/O requests on a swap device by keeping reclaim batches contiguous. The current implementation of swap allocation and deallocation can lead to scattered writes, resulting in increased I/O requests. The patch modifies the allocator to allocate contiguous free slots for a reclaim batch, reducing the number of small requests and improving throughput. This is achieved by informing the allocator about the size of the batch and allowing it to allocate contiguous slots accordingly. The goal is to reduce the overhead of swap I/O operations and improve system performance.

review_comments.author: Kairui Song
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Kairui Song suggested reverting commit 9a42aed48421, which prefers nonfull over free clusters for small order allocations, and instead always scanning full clusters to prioritize contiguity on large physical swap devices.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Alexandre,

That's a interesting problem. I think the real problem is with commit
9a42aed48421 ("mm, swap: prefer nonfull over free clusters"), right?

It's more like a balance between fragmentation and contiguity of small
order allocation issue.

Perhaps we should instead always scan the full clusters and revert
that one commit? That commit was only following the idea of keeping
the allocation more compacted for that series, it looked good at that
time. Since fragmentation issues can be solved in other ways,
contiguity seems to matter more for large physical swap devices.

What are the other fragmentation solutions you are referring to?

Alex

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concerns that the proposed solution of allocating contiguous swap slots may not address the underlying issue and could lead to increased memory overhead, scanning overhead, etc., suggesting that physical swap space compaction is still a problem and virtual swap space would just shift the issue.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hmm what other way are you thinking of? Physical swap space compaction
requires vswap, which has not landed. And we'd just be kicking the
problem to virtual swap space. Sure, we won't be failing allocation,
but that would still increase the memory overhead, scanning overhead,
etc.

I encountered this myself. Remember when I wrote my own swap allocator
for vswap? In one of the version, I went for free clusters first
instead of partial clusters. It fragmented the swap space, so I had to
copy your homework and went for partially used clusters first...

Anyway, maybe I'm wrong - some numbers would be nice here.

review_comments.author: Kairui Song
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer suggested limiting the patch's scope to SYNC devices or exploring simpler solutions to address the problem, expressing skepticism about the significance of a 4% reduction in mTHP failures.

Reviewer Kairui Song suggested addressing swap space fragmentation by sorting clusters by slot size before moving them back to the non-full list, which would mitigate the issue until a more comprehensive solution is implemented.
review_comments.raw_body:
That patch is 1/3 of a series, that series yields really nice
results, but that one patch plays only a small part in them. Or
perhaps we can limit that to SYNC devices? I hope there are simpler
ways to avoid the problem you encountered. I think the ~4% reduction
of 64k mTHP failure is kind of trivial compared to the problem you
encountered, and 2M swapout is still not easily doable, as the
main blocker is from the page allocator.

Right, nothing has landed in upstream for that yet, but with larger

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] mm/mempolicy: recompute automatic interleave weights on memory hotplug

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm/mempolicy: recompute automatic interleave weights on memory hotplug

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch updates the automatic interleave weights in Linux's memory policy when a node gains or loses memory due to hotplug events. The current implementation only recalculates the weights when a new bandwidth is reported, which can lead to incorrect weights being used for some nodes. This patch introduces a new function `wi_state_refresh` that recomputes the weights from the recorded bandwidth whenever a node gains its first memory or loses its last. This ensures that the weighted interleave algorithm always uses accurate and up-to-date weights, leading to improved performance in certain scenarios.

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm/vmscan: reclaim every zone in per-node proactive reclaim

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the per-node proactive reclaim function to scan every zone, not just ZONE_NORMAL, in order to reclaim movable memory as well. This addresses a problem where nodes with only movable memory were not being reclaimed properly. The approach taken is to change the `reclaim_idx` field of the `scan_control` structure to always set it to the maximum number of zones, allowing all zones to be scanned.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/2] memcg: reduce cacheline contention between lruvec stat updates and LRU lists
series_items.patch_summary: This patch reduces cacheline contention between lruvec stat updates and LRU lists by rearranging the layout of struct mem_cgroup_per_node in memory. The goal is to minimize unnecessary overhead caused by spatial prefetching on Intel CPUs, which can lead to increased lock contention and slower performance. The patch achieves this by moving the 'memcg_pn_cold' group after 'memcg_pn_read_mostly', ensuring that the read-mostly cacheline is paired with the cold cacheline instead of the LRU list heads. This change was validated through benchmarking, which showed a significant reduction in contention and improved performance.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/2] memcg: don't go through the lruvec for folio and kmem lruvec stat updates
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes memory cgroup (memcg) statistics updates by bypassing the lruvec data structure for folio and kmem lruvec stat updates. It directly passes the memcg and node to the mod_memcg_node_state function, reducing contention with other threads that access the lru_lock holder. This change improves throughput in certain scenarios, such as on a 2-socket Skylake system with multiple threads accessing shared memory.

review_comments.author: Michal Hocko
review_comments.summary: Gave Acked-by

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch reduces cacheline contention between lruvec stat updates and LRU lists by rearranging the layout of struct mem_cgroup_per_node to pair read-mostly lines with cold lines, and modifying folio and kmem stat updates to avoid going through the lruvec. This change improves performance on systems that use spatial prefetching, such as Intel CPUs. The patch includes two changes: one that reorders the fields in struct mem_cgroup_per_node, and another that modifies the stat update functions to skip using the lruvec. The results show a significant improvement in pages per second for threads faulting in and freeing memory in a single memcg.

review_comments.author: Andrew Morton
review_comments.summary: The reviewer noted that even though the patch rearranges struct mem_cgroup_per_node to pair its read-mostly line with a cold line, it does not guarantee that every read-mostly line will be paired with a cold line due to SLAB_HWCACHE_ALIGN slab usage, which can align objects to 128-byte boundaries but still allow adjacent objects to share a cacheline pair.
review_comments.raw_body:
Thanks.  A local AI review pointed out a thing:

  One limitation worth mentioning in the [1/2] changelog: the slab
  uses SLAB_HWCACHE_ALIGN, which need not align each object to a
  128-byte boundary.  If an object starts 64 bytes into such a pair,
  its first line can still be paired with the end of the preceding
  object rather than its own cold line.  This isn't a correctness
  issue, and the measured Skylake improvement may well be real, but the
  layout doesn't guarantee that every read-mostly line pairs with a
  cold line.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 1/5] mm/memcontrol: flatten try_charge_memcg control flow
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the try_charge_memcg function in mm/memcontrol.c to simplify its control flow by separating the logic for memsw and memory page counters into distinct paths. This makes it easier to follow the code, especially after making page_counter_try_charge stock-aware. The change does not introduce any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 2/5] mm/page_counter: introduce per-CPU stock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a per-CPU stock representation in the page_counter layer, similar to memcg's seven-slot per-CPU stock. It adds a new struct page_counter_stock_pcp that preserves the existing behavior from memcg and includes a backpointer to the base of the percpu stock. The patch also updates the page_counter structure to include pointers to the percpu stock and its owning cgroup_subsys_state. No functional changes are intended in this patch, which is part of a larger series.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 3/5] mm/page_counter: make page_counter_try_charge() stock-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the page_counter_try_charge() function to be aware of stock, allowing it to consume stock transparently while preserving existing semantics. Two new parameters are added: may_batch and nr_charged. The first parameter preserves the behavior of !allow_spinning scenarios in try_charge_memcg, where charges are made as quickly as possible without evicting other stock slots or making a greedy charge to refill the stock. The second parameter reflects the size of the successful hierarchy charge, preserving batch-based memory.high accounting for current->memcg_nr_pages_over_high.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 4/5] mm/memcontrol: move memory stock to page counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the memory stock from memcg to page counters, allowing for more efficient management of memory usage. The change affects how memory and swap counters interact, potentially causing temporary divergence in their raw values. To maintain compatibility, the patch introduces a new logic to ensure that reclaim doesn't swap when memory fails first, even if memory and swap have equal limits. The patch also removes unused memcg code and preserves existing behaviors for cgroup v2 users. The change sets the stage for future work on introducing additional page counters without breaking the fast path.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 5/5] mm/memcontrol: add stock to the memsw page counter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a separate stock to the memsw page counter, allowing it to operate independently of the memory bank. The common drain scheduling is factored into schedule_stock_drain(), which handles charge, refill, and hotplug operations for both stocks. If memory charge fails, only nr_pages from memsw are rolled back. The patch also preserves the user-visible cgroup-v1 memory invariant by reporting memory.usage_in_bytes as the smaller raw value.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series moves the stock management from mem_cgroup to page_counter, allowing each page_counter to have its own per-CPU cache of pre-charged pages. This change is necessary for future work on scalable and performant page_counters, such as the tiered memcg limits series. The decoupling of memory and memsw stocks in cgroup v1 users may lead to different sizes of precharged caches, but the patch preserves the invariant that memory.usage_in_bytes is less than or equal to memory.memsw.usage_in_bytes by reporting the smaller value. This change has no functional impact on memcg v2 users.

implications to caching at different levels of the hierarchy? An example
of cache propagation up/down the hierarchy during
charge/uncharge/draining would be really useful to wrap ones head around
how this is supposed to work.

review_comments.author: Joshua Hahn (author)
review_comments.summary:
The author is addressing concerns about the patch's impact on cgroupv2, specifically how it will interact with new page_counters being added to struct memcg. The author acknowledges that the current implementation of stocking charge for memcg is equivalent to stocking charge for the memcg->memory page_counter and explains that their ongoing work adds new per-tier page_counters to struct memcg, which cannot use the stock fastpath due to its inability to distinguish memory residence. They argue that their patch avoids hierarchy walks for most charges.

Author agrees that additional context is needed and plans to provide it by adding call traces, indicating that no fix is currently planned but more information will be provided.

Author addressed a concern about the impact of separate stocking on cgroup v1 users by explaining that memory.usage_in_bytes will be reported as the smaller of raw memory and memsw values to preserve the invariant.

Author acknowledged that cgroup v2 users should not see any changes in the patch series and offered to provide additional explanation on how stocking currently works.

The author is addressing concerns about the behavior of reporting memory usage when memsw and memory stocks are decoupled. He acknowledges that there can be an inversion where memsw reports a higher usage than memory, but explains that this is due to how direct charging works in such scenarios. The author proposes fuzzily reporting the minimum of the two reported values, which he claims aligns with the existing fuzzy nature of usage_in_bytes.
review_comments.raw_body:
So right now for cgroupv2, there's kind of a 1-1 mapping between
page_counter and memcg. I say "kind of" because there still is a
page_counter for swap, but it takes a completely different charging
path (i.e. not try_charge_memcg).

This means that currently stocking charge for memcg is equivalent to
stocking charge for the memcg->memory page_counter.

However, one of the series that I'm currently working on [1] adds new
page_counters to struct memcg to track the usage of memory
per-memcg, per-tier. The goal is to (1) track how much memory of a
cgroup lives on which tier, and (2) to limit the usage so that a single
cgroup doesn't use up all the fast tier memory alone, and shares it
fairly with all the other cgroups on the host.

When adding a new per-tier page_counter to struct mem_cgroup that gets
charged for every memcg_charge, I cannot use the stock fastpath since
the stock does not distinguish where the memory resides. It would
essentialy boil down to this pattern:

try_charge_memcg
   \__ page_couner_try_charge(memcg->tier[0])
   \__ consume_stock()

Where every path still has to do a hierarchy charge to the tier it's
charging to, whereas this patch gets us:

try_charge_memcg
   \__ page_counter_try_charge(memcg->tier[0])
          \__ consume_stock(memcg->tier[0])
   \__ page_countertry_charge(memcg->memory)
          \__ consume_stock(memcg->memory)

So that we can avoid the hierarchy walk for most charges.

I'd be happy to submit a new cover letter which better explains this
idea!

---

Sounds good with me. I can add the call traces above which should
explain my thought process a bit more. Hopefully the problem I am
trying to solve is evident there.

---

No changes to locking. In fact this series is mostly just moving code
from mm/memcontrol.c to mm/page_counter.c, everything is essentially
the same.

---

This series should not have any changes for cgroup v2, including when
and where the cache is stocked / drained in the hierarchy. I can
include a snippet on how stocking currently works to add a visual
explanation, if that helps too.

---

Yeah, so this part is a little bit annoying. Let's just look at a single
leaf cgroup for example, where the limit for memsw and memory are both
64 pages.

charge_memcg(64)
	raw memory: 64			raw memsw: 64
	reported memory: 64		reported memsw: 64
	memory stock: 0			memory stock: 0

swap out 32 pages
	raw memory: 32			raw memsw: 64
	reported memory: 32		reported memsw: 64
	memory stock: 0			memsw stock: 0

free 32 pages
	raw memory: 0			raw memsw: 32
	reported memory: 0		reported memsw: 32
	memory stock: 0			memsw stock: 0

charge_memcg(1)
	raw memory: 1			raw memsw: 33
	reported memory: 64		reported memsw: 33
	memory stock: 63		memsw stock: 0

Where the last charge_memcg() causes the inversion. memsw tries to
charge a batch of 64 to refill the stock, but fails since 32+64=96
puts the memsw over its max limit. So it falls back to direct charging
where it charges the page_counter directly, and ends up with 0 stock
and reporting a usage of 33.

On the other hand, memory will greedily refill the stock with 64 pages
and since usage is 0, the batch refill will succeed, and it will report
a usage of 64.

So the idea with reporting the minimum is to report the minimum of the
two reported values, we will just fuzzily report the stocked value.
IIRC usage_in_bytes has always been fuzzy anyways, due to how much
memory has been stocked.

Thanks again for taking a look, Michal! I hope you have a great day : -)
Joshua

patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the Linux kernel's atomic operations by allowing faults to occur when updating a read-only HVO (Hardware Virtualization Optimization) tail page, rather than attempting to handle speculative gets. The fix involves introducing a new function, arch_atomic_fetch_add_unless_nofault(), which allows faults to be handled instead of oopsing. This change is specific to x86, RISC-V, and LoongArch architectures, which support HVO. The patch has been lightly tested on x86 by hitting a real HVO tail page.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author acknowledges a real bug in the current implementation and explains that their initial reasoning was incorrect. They propose to fix this by letting the atomic fault, which would handle the case where the struct page is a read-only HVO tail with a zero refcount. The author has lightly tested this on x86 and suggests preparing a proper patchset if the idea looks reasonable.
review_comments.raw_body:
Ughh. Yes, it is a real bug.

My reasoning in the commit message was wrong. Nothing stops a
speculative get from writing to one after the remap. On x86 even a
failing cmpxchg faults there.

The fix I have in mind is to let the atomic fault.

If the update faults, the struct page is a read-only HVO tail with a
zero refcount, so the get just fails. An exception table entry on the
cmpxchg handles it. No RCU on either side, and the fast path stays the
same lock cmpxchg loop.

Only x86, riscv and loongarch have HVO. Below is x86 only, to show the
idea; riscv and loongarch need the same primitive in their LL/SC
fetch_add_unless().

Lightly tested on x86 by hitting a real HVO tail page.

Does it look sane?

I can prepare a proper patchset if looks reasonable.

diff --git a/arch/x86/include/asm/atomic.h b/arch/x86/include/asm/atomic.h
index 75743f1dfd4e..5252b1382ed0 100644
--- a/arch/x86/include/asm/atomic.h
+++ b/arch/x86/include/asm/atomic.h
@@ -108,6 +108,25 @@ static __always_inline bool arch_atomic_try_cmpxchg(atomic_t *v, int *old, int n
 }
 #define arch_atomic_try_cmpxchg arch_atomic_try_cmpxchg
 
+/*
+ * arch_atomic_fetch_add_unless_nofault() is arch_atomic_fetch_add_unless(),
+ * except that a fault on the access jumps to @label instead of oopsing.  It
+ * works in any context, including with IRQs disabled.
+ */
+#define arch_atomic_fetch_add_unless_nofault(_v, _a, _u, label)	\
+({									\
+	atomic_t *__v = (_v);						\
+	int __a = (_a), __u = (_u);					\
+	int __c = arch_atomic_read(__v);				\
+									\
+	do {								\
+		if (unlikely(__c == __u))				\
+			break;						\
+	} while (!__try_cmpxchg_nofault(&__v->counter, &__c,		\
+					__c + __a, label));		\
+	__c;								\
+})
+
 static __always_inline int arch_atomic_xchg(atomic_t *v, int new)
 {
 	return arch_xchg(&v->counter, new);
diff --git a/arch/x86/include/asm/cmpxchg.h b/arch/x86/include/asm/cmpxchg.h
index a88b06f1c35e..685aab3edd3f 100644
--- a/arch/x86/include/asm/cmpxchg.h
+++ b/arch/x86/include/asm/cmpxchg.h
@@ -232,6 +232,63 @@ extern void __add_wrong_size(void)
 #define arch_try_cmpxchg_local(ptr, pold, new)				\
 	__try_cmpxchg_local((ptr), (pold), (new), sizeof(*(ptr)))
 
+/*
+ * __try_cmpxchg_nofault() is arch_try_cmpxchg() on a 4-byte kernel variable,
+ * except that a fault on the access jumps to @label instead of oopsing.
+ */
+#ifdef CONFIG_CC_HAS_ASM_GOTO_TIED_OUTPUT
+#define __try_cmpxchg_nofault(_ptr, _pold, _new, label)		\
+({									\
+	bool success;							\
+	__typeof__(_ptr) _old = (__typeof__(_ptr))(_pold);		\
+	__typeof__(*(_ptr)) __old = *_old;				\
+	__typeof__(*(_ptr)) __new = (_new);				\
+									\
+	if (sizeof(*(_ptr)) != 4)					\
+		__cmpxchg_wrong_size();					\
+	asm_goto_output("\n"						\
+			"1: " LOCK_PREFIX "cmpxchgl %[new], %[ptr]\n"	\
+			_ASM_EXTABLE(1b, %l[label])			\
+			: "=@ccz" (success),				\
+			  [ptr] "+m" (*(_ptr)),				\
+			  [old] "+a" (__old)				\
+			: [new] "r" (__new)				\
+			: "memory"					\
+			: label);					\
+	if (unlikely(!success))						\
+		*_old = __old;						\
+	likely(success);						\
+})
+#else
+#define __try_cmpxchg_nofault(_ptr, _pold, _new, label)		\
+({									\
+	int __err = 0;							\
+	bool success;							\
+	__typeof__(_ptr) _old = (__typeof__(_ptr))(_pold);		\
+	__typeof__(*(_ptr)) __old = *_old;				\
+	__typeof__(*(_ptr)) __new = (_new);				\
+									\
+	if (sizeof(*(_ptr)) != 4)					\
+		__cmpxchg_wrong_size();					\
+	asm volatile("\n"						\
+		     "1: " LOCK_PREFIX "cmpxchgl %[new], %[ptr]\n"	\
+		     "2:\n"						\
+		     _ASM_EXTABLE_TYPE_REG(1b, 2b, EX_TYPE_EFAULT_REG,	\
+					   %[errout])			\
+		     : "=@ccz" (success),				\
+		       [errout] "+r" (__err),				\
+		       [ptr] "+m" (*(_ptr)),				\
+		       [old] "+a" (__old)				\
+		     : [new] "r" (__new)				\
+		     : "memory");					\
+	if (unlikely(__err))						\
+		goto label;						\
+	if (unlikely(!success))						\
+		*_old = __old;						\
+	likely(success);						\
+})
+#endif
+
 /*
  * xadd() adds "inc" to "*ptr" and atomically returns the previous
  * value of "*ptr".
diff --git a/include/linux/page_ref.h b/include/linux/page_ref.h
index 9f5c75d06f76..82a2fc445ce6 100644
--- a/include/linux/page_ref.h
+++ b/include/linux/page_ref.h
@@ -246,9 +246,31 @@ static inline int folio_ref_dec_return(struct folio *folio)
 	return page_ref_dec_return(&folio->page);
 }
 
+#ifdef CONFIG_HUGETLB_PAGE_OPTIMIZE_VMEMMAP
+/*
+ * HVO maps the tail struct pages of a hugetlb folio read-only.  A speculative
+ * caller can read a non-zero refcount, then the page gets freed, becomes a
+ * tail page of a hugetlb folio and is remapped before the update.  The
+ * atomic then faults.  A read-only struct page is a hugetlb tail page with a
+ * zero refcount, so the fault means no reference can be taken.
+ */
+static __always_inline bool __page_ref_add_unless_zero(atomic_t *v, int nr)
+{
+	instrument_atomic_read_write(v, sizeof(*v));
+	return arch_atomic_fetch_add_unless_nofault(v, nr, 0, fault) != 0;
+fault:
+	return false;
+}
+#else
+static __always_inline bool __page_ref_add_unless_zero(atomic_t *v, int nr)
+{
+	return atomic_add_unless(v, nr, 0);
+}
+#endif
+
 static inline bool page_ref_add_unless_zero(struct page *page, int nr)
 {
-	bool ret = atomic_add_unless(&page->_refcount, nr, 0);
+	bool ret = __page_ref_add_unless_zero(&page->_refcount, nr);
 
 	if (page_ref_tracepoint_active(page_ref_mod_unless))
 		__page_ref_mod_unless(page, nr, ret);
-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

http://lists.infradead.org/mailman/listinfo/linux-riscv

Re: [PATCH] shmem: do not extend i_size when no data was copied
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: Patch aims to prevent i_size extension when no data is copied, but raises questions about the correct location for the fix.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau
review_comments.summary: Raised concerns about the patch's scope and suggested that generic_perform_write() might be a better place to fix the issue.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Mon, Oct 26, 2026 at 04:48:58PM +0100, Jan Kara wrote:
> On Mon 26-10-26 15:34:08, Kiryl Shutsemau wrote:
> > On Sun, Oct 25, 2026 at 04:46:19PM +0000, Hungyu Lin wrote:
> > > shmem_write_end() advances i_size to pos + copied even when copied is
> > > zero. A buffered write past EOF can therefore extend a tmpfs file
> > > without writing any data.
> > 
> > + willy, jack, fsdevel.
> > 
> > This doesn't seem to be tmpfs-specific, right? I see the same with ext4.
> > 
> > simple_write_end() and generic_write_end() check pos + copied the same
> > way, so filesystems that use them through generic_perform_write() are
> > affected too.
> > 
> > It makes me think maybe generic_perform_write() is the right place to
> > fix it. Hm?
> 
> Well, that would be nice. But how'd you like to do that? i_size update is
> the responsibility of ->write_end and we have to call ->write_end if copied
> == 0 so that is undoes what ->write_begin has prepared.

Hm.

A zero-length copy only moves i_size if the write starts beyond EOF.
So we can bring the prefault back just for that case, before
->write_begin():

        if (unlikely(pos > i_size_read(mapping->host)) &&
            fault_in_iov_iter_readable(i, bytes) == bytes) {
                status = -EFAULT;
                break;
        }

Overwrites and appends keep skipping the prefault. It is racy against
a concurrent munmap(), as it was before 665575cff098, but that is
userspace racing with itself.

The per-filesystem alternative is a 'copied &&' in every ->write_end.

And generic_write_end() cannot take it as is: generic_cont_expand_simple()
relies on a zero-length ->write_end() extending i_size. So we need some
replacement.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

review_comments.summary: Agreed that the patch is a good idea, but pointed out that i_size update is the responsibility of ->write_end and suggested that the fix should undo what ->write_begin has prepared.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Mon 26-10-26 15:34:08, Kiryl Shutsemau wrote:
> On Sun, Oct 25, 2026 at 04:46:19PM +0000, Hungyu Lin wrote:
> > shmem_write_end() advances i_size to pos + copied even when copied is
> > zero. A buffered write past EOF can therefore extend a tmpfs file
> > without writing any data.
> 
> + willy, jack, fsdevel.
> 
> This doesn't seem to be tmpfs-specific, right? I see the same with ext4.
> 
> simple_write_end() and generic_write_end() check pos + copied the same
> way, so filesystems that use them through generic_perform_write() are
> affected too.
> 
> It makes me think maybe generic_perform_write() is the right place to
> fix it. Hm?

Well, that would be nice. But how'd you like to do that? i_size update is
the responsibility of ->write_end and we have to call ->write_end if copied
== 0 so that is undoes what ->write_begin has prepared.

								Honza

SUSE Labs, CR

review_comments.author: Zi Yan
review_comments.summary: Pointed out that Zhang Yi's truncate fix already achieves the suggested explicit split state communication.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Mon Oct 26, 2026 at 1:26 PM EDT, Kiryl Shutsemau wrote:
> On Mon, Oct 26, 2026 at 10:40:44AM +0100, David Hildenbrand (Arm) wrote:
>> The final scan in shmem_undo_range() restarts after a successful split
>> only if the original folio is no longer large. A nonuniform split can
>> leave that folio large, so the scan skips the newly created folios.
>> Hole punching then leaves pages within the hole allocated even though
>> they could be discarded.
>> 
>> For example, a fault below the hole can allocate a 2 MiB folio after
>> boundary handling. Punching a 1 MiB hole at offset 64 KiB splits the
>> folio successfully but leaves the original folio at order 4. The scan
>> continues past all 512 pages, leaving 2 MiB allocated instead of 1 MiB.
>> The hole reads as zero, but the pages and their block charges remain.
>> 
>> Restart when the original folio is still in the mapping after partial
>> truncation, identified by checking folio->mapping. If the helper
>> removed the whole folio, no rescan is needed.
>> 
>> Fixes: 7460b470a131f ("mm/truncate: use folio_split() in truncate operation")
>> Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
>> Signed-off-by: David Hildenbrand (Arm) <david@kernel.org>
>
> Acked-by: Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) <kas@kernel.org>
>
> Do we want split state after truncate_inode_partial_folio() to be
> communicated more explicit? ->mapping check works, but it might not be
> obvious why. Just an idea for a follow up.

Zhang Yi's truncate fix has done that. truncate_inode_partial_folio()
returns true only if the folio is split[1]. His patches are in mm-stable
but not upstreamed yet.

[1] https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/akpm/mm.git/tree/mm/truncate.c?h=mm-stable#n248

-- 
Best Regards,
Yan, Zi

patches_submitted.subject: [RFC PATCH] x86,resctrl: Read event counters with an IPI when the read cannot block

version_history.subject: [RFC PATCH] x86,resctrl: Read event counters with an IPI when the read cannot block

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new configuration option CONFIG_RESCTRL_MON_READ_IRQSAFE to allow reading event counters with interrupts off on the current CPU or using an IPI when necessary. This is done to reduce long stalls caused by readers sleeping while holding rdtgroup_mutex, which can lead to gaps in monitoring data. The patch adds support for x86 architecture and provides results showing a significant reduction in hold time per read and time off CPU while holding the mutex.

review_comments.author: Reinette Chatre
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Reinette Chatre pointed out that the patch does not handle the case where CONFIG_RESCTRL_MON_READ_IRQSAFE is disabled, which would cause a regression on architectures other than x86.

Reviewer noted that the patch's solution for high-performance monitoring is overly aggressive, given the existing limitations of the resctrl mon_data files interface.

Reviewer Reinette Chatre asked Shakeel Butt to consider the thread that followed his previous proposal, implying that there may be relevant information or context that was not addressed in the current patch.

Reviewer Reinette Chatre noted that the proposed patch only slightly adjusts the limit of how many monitor groups this deployment can support, and suggested considering a per-group rate as proposed by Peter Newman to enable full capability of the systems.

Reviewer noted that reading 128 MON groups with interrupts off can take up to 131 us, which may be significant for applications where the kernel is also monitoring itself.

Reviewer questioned the necessity of reading event counters every 100 ms, suggesting that the overflow handler's one-second interval is sufficient for querying data

Reviewer noted that the patch does not fully address the scalability issue for large numbers of monitoring groups, and suggested considering per-group rate files as a potential solution.

Reviewer Reinette Chatre suggested avoiding a config option and instead making read_irq_safe a per-resource property, citing concerns about the scope of change as multiple architectural drivers are involved.

Reviewer noted that the patch's use of raw_ functions to disable preemption is only effective when preemption is disabled, and suggested it may be a re-implementation of smp_call_function_any()

Reviewer Reinette Chatre noted that the '!tick_nohz_full_cpu(this_cpu)' check in the patch defeats its own goal of preventing an IPI when a reader is pinned to the domain, and suggested reordering the logic to prefer the current CPU whenever it's in the domain, nohz_full or not.
sentiment_signals: scope of change will be significant
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Shakeel,

On 10/20/26 8:13 AM, Shakeel Butt wrote:

---

This is very demanding usage of an interface that cannot and has never 
intended to be fast.

---

Did you consider the thread that followed that proposal to learn why it did
not land?

---

The numbers make the contention clear. If I got the math right the "after"
is still about 10us per file and with 4us spent holding rdtgroup_mutex there
is still about 6us per file spent outside resctrl. I expect this is
taken up by the syscalls, the various kernfs allocations to manage the read
cycle, also a seq_buf allocation of a page (just to return a few bytes of data).

I do not think the 750 file example accurately captures how "bad" things
can get. From what I can tell this proposal only *slightly* adjusts the limit
of how many monitor groups this deployment can support.

My guess is that the 750 file example looks like possibly about 25 monitor
groups with three events each monitored across 10 domains.

The "after" value indicates that this deployment can now support more monitoring
groups. For example, 250 monitor groups with a pass over the increased number
of files taking about 74ms.

AMD can support 4096 monitor groups though so while this change is undeniably
an improvement, it does not address the foundational limitations of this
interface and does not enable this deployment to use full capability of
the systems.

If the goal is indeed to obtain accurate monitoring data at regular
intervals when using the stated hardware at its full capacity then
I would suggest that you consider the per-group rate files that Peter
settled on per
https://lore.kernel.org/all/CALPaoCgpnVORZfbKVLXDFUZvv8jhpShHPzB3cwdLTZQH1o9ULw@mail.gmail.com/

I actually cannot remember seeing an update on that work after he posted that
message and my assumption has been that that is what they have been using since
then.

Essentially the solution builds on the monitoring data already collected by the
per-domain overflow handler, it turns that data into a rate that user space can
read on demand without any IPI.

---

128 MON groups sound low - it looks like AMD has 4096 possible MON groups.

Interrupting a monitored application with interrupts off for so long
is significant for a fleet whose product is the monitored application.

---

Is it really needed to get the data every 100ms? The overflow handler runs
every second and the data could just be queried from it.

---

...

As I understand this patch slightly moves the needle on how many monitoring
groups this deployment can support. I do not believe this patch enables this
deployment to support all monitoring groups possible. 

Please do consider per-group rate files as discussed in the thread around [4].

Even so, surely this patch improves performance under some scenarios. We could continue
to consider it if you still believe it useful.

---

Please avoid a config option. This could be a per-resource property,
for example, rdt_resource::mon::read_irq_safe (I'll defer naming debates).
I'd recommend against an architectural helper like [4] since now that there
are multiple architectural drivers the scope of change will be significant since
it spans across branches that take different routes upstream.

---

hmmm ... this is meaningless without preemption disabled, no? Looks like this
uses raw_ to get around the CONFIG_DEBUG_PREEMPT check :(

On the face of this it seems to attempt a re-implementation of smp_call_function_any()?

---

Doesn't this "!tick_nohz_full_cpu(this_cpu)" check defeat one major goal of this
patch, which is to prevent an IPI if a reader pinned itself to the domain? A monitoring
data reader may very well pin itself to a CPU in the monitoring domain and be running
on a nohz_full CPU.

It looks like the rule should be "prefer the current CPU whenever it is in the domain,
nohz_full or not"?

On first glance I wonder if this could be re-ordered. I surely need to think about this
more but how about something like below:


	if (r->mon.read_irq_safe) {
                  /*
                   * Reading the counter does not sleep, it only has to run on a
                   * CPU in the domain. Prefer the current CPU when it is one:
                   * the counter can be read without an IPI and without
                   * disturbing any other CPU. A nohz_full current CPU is not
                   * avoided, the reasons to avoid nohz_full CPUs, interrupting
                   * user space and queueing work that may never run, do not
                   * apply to the CPU making this request.
                   *
                   * Preemption is disabled for the test because the answer is
                   * only valid while this task cannot migrate. It is enabled
                   * again before the IPI to let other work run while waiting.
                   */
                  cpu = get_cpu();
                  if (!cpumask_test_cpu(cpu, cpumask))
                          cpu = cpumask_any_housekeeping(cpumask,
                                                         RESCTRL_PICK_ANY_CPU);
                  put_cpu();

                  smp_call_function_single(cpu, mon_event_count, rr, 1);
                  goto out_ctx_free;
          }

          cpu = cpumask_any_housekeeping(cpumask, RESCTRL_PICK_ANY_CPU);		
	 ...

review_comments.author: Peter Newman
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Peter Newman noted that the patch does not handle the case where the target CPU is in a nohz_full domain, and requested that an IPI be sent to wake up the kworker on the target CPU.

Reviewer Peter Newman expressed concerns about the practicality of implementing the patch, citing existing issues with MBM implementations on AMD and a preference to use the offcore PMU instead.

Reviewer pointed out that interrupt masking has a limited impact on latency since interrupts are reenabled between counter reads, and instead highlighted the issue of workload scheduling being impacted by this feature, suggesting it would need to be disabled in nohz_full mode for high-availability products.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, Oct 22, 2026 at 12:58 AM Reinette Chatre
<reinette.chatre@intel.com> wrote:

---

These changes have been available within Google for a while, but I
don't believe they've ever gone into use. They've had a lot of other
issues with the MBM implementations on AMD and have been estimating
jobs' bandwidth using the offcore PMU instead.

Shakeel, I can share the changes for you to try out, but they won't be
up to the standard for code review. If it works for you, that would be
one confirmed user and I could put more time into it.

---

Interrupts are reenabled between counter reads, so the cumulative time
interrupts are masked doesn't impact latency.

The time the customer's workload wasn't scheduled was a bigger issue,
though. On the higher-availability products, this was feature would
need to be disabled by an entire domain running in nohz_full mode.

-Peter

review_comments.author: Shakeel Butt (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author acknowledged that the current implementation of CONFIG_RESCTRL_MON_READ_IRQSAFE does not handle the case where every CPU in the domain is nohz_full and agreed to add a check for this condition.

Author acknowledged that a critical reader of the interface is experiencing multi-second stalls, which causes gaps in system observability, and agreed to address this issue.

Author acknowledges the reviewer's concern about potential performance impact, but prioritizes avoiding critical daemons being stuck behind lower-priority readers.

The author acknowledges that the patch does not address scalability issues, but explains that its purpose is to reduce hold time and uncertainty by changing how locks are held during sleeping.

Author acknowledged the need to address the rate file interface and agreed to review Peter's prototype.

Author acknowledges that some userspace applications may be impacted by the proposed change, but notes that other applications like below and dynolog read less often and are not as affected.

Author acknowledges that the existing rate file tools are complementary to the mon_data files and agrees to address all reviewer suggestions in the next patch version.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Reinette,

Thanks for the detailed review and feedback and sorry for late response.

On Wed, Oct 21, 2026 at 03:58:38PM -0700, Reinette Chatre wrote:

---

I think I agree here and I should have been more clear about my motivation. The
actual issue I am trying to resolve is that one of the reader of this interface
(actually below) is very critical for reliability of the system (or actually
observability) and we are seeing multi-second stalls in that daemon on this
interface. This causes gaps in our observability into the issues.

Also I think the read rates are modest. Below reads the whole tree every 5
seconds and scx_layered reads one root-group file per domain every 100ms.

[...]

---

Yes and I think the problem I am tring to solve is a bit different. I am ok with
spending more cpu cycles in order to avoid critical daemon getting stuck behind
lower priority readers and may get impacted by scheduling delays or priority
inversion.

---

Yes you are right. The patch does not change how a full sweep scales. It is only
changing the potential hold time of the sleeping locks and today it depends on
scheduling on another CPU which introduced a lot of uncertainty.

---

I will think more about rate file interface. It seems like Peter has offered his
prototype, I will take a look.

---

Most probably not. I have to check with scx_layered folks if they really need 100ms.
However below and dynolog reads less often and are impacted by stalls on this
path most of the time.

---

I will and I still feel the rate file are complementary as the existing tools
use the mon_data files and this patch helps them.

I will address all of your suggestions/concerns on the code in the next version.

Again, thanks a lot of the detailed and helpful feedback.
